title: Where are you from?
goal: Say where you're from, where you live, and which languages you speak; then face one big difference from English: the word "not" sits AFTER the verb, with no "do" to lean on.
bekal: ask and answer where someone is from with *hvaðan* and *frá*
make any sentence negative by putting *ekki* in the right place
say you're in the middle of doing something with *ég er að …*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Í kaffihúsi
dialogs.intro: The next day, in a café on Laugavegur street. Anna is reading when Búdí walks by and sits down with her.

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.text: Ég er frá Indónesíu, frá Jakarta.
lines.literal: I am from Indonesia, from Jakarta.

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.id: Do you live in Reykjavík now?

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.text: Já, ég bý í Reykjavík. Ég bý ekki í Jakarta lengur.
lines.id: Yes, I live in Reykjavík. I don't live in Jakarta anymore.
lines.literal: yes, I live in Reykjavík. I live not in Jakarta longer.

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.text: Ég tala indónesísku og ensku. Ég tala ekki þýsku.
lines.id: I speak Indonesian and English. I don't speak German.
lines.literal: I speak Indonesian and English. I speak not German.

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.text: Ég er að læra. Það er erfitt en skemmtilegt.
lines.id: I'm learning. It's hard but fun.
lines.literal: I am to learn. it is hard but fun.

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Íslenska er ekki erfið, hún er bara ný fyrir þig!
lines.id: Icelandic isn't hard, it's just new to you!
lines.literal: Icelandic is not hard, she is only new for you!

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Ég er að lesa. Ég er íslenskukennari.
lines.id: I'm reading. I'm an Icelandic teacher.
lines.literal: I am to read. I am Icelandic-teacher.

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.text: Nei, er það satt? Þá þarf ég hjálp!
lines.id: No way, really? Then I need help!
lines.literal: no, is it true? then need I help!

notes: **Ekki sits AFTER the verb.** *Ég tala ekki þýsku* — literally "I speak not German". English needs a helper and puts "not" in front of the main verb ("I don't speak"); Icelandic has no "do" and simply follows the verb with *ekki*. Practice the pairs as one sound: *tala-ekki*, *bý-ekki*, *er-ekki*.
**Býrðu = býr + þú.** The glued-on *þú* shows up again, this time on verbs ending in -r: *býrðu*, *talarðu*, *lærirðu*. The **ð** in the middle is what's left of a melted *þ*.

**Ég er að læra literally "I am to learn".** This is the "-ing" form — and Icelandic is **the only Nordic language** with a progressive like the English *-ing*. The pattern never changes: *vera* + *að* + the infinitive.

**Language names change form after tala.** The basic forms are *íslenska*, *enska*, *þýska*; after *tala* the ending becomes **-u**: *tala íslensku*, *tala ensku*, *tala þýsku*. You're seeing the **þolfall** case for the first time; it gets its name in Unit 8.

**Erfitt, erfið, erfiður — one adjective, three forms.** The form follows the gender of the word it describes: *það er erfitt* (neuter), *íslenska er erfið* (feminine), *tími er erfiður* (masculine). These three noun genders are what Unit 3 is about.

**Nei, er það satt? is not a denial.** Literally "no, is that true?", but it works exactly like "No way, really?" — a pleased expression of surprise. Icelanders use it several times in one conversation.

grammars.title: Ekki — fixed place, clear meaning
body: One word for every kind of "not", and it almost always stands right **after the verb**.
after: ⚠️ If the object is a **pronoun** (*þig*, *hana*, *það*), *ekki* jumps behind it: *Ég skil þig ekki*. If the object is an ordinary noun, *ekki* stays in front: *Ég skil bókina ekki* also sounds natural, but *Ég skil ekki bókina* is more common.

Answering a negative question: if you really **can't**, answer *nei*; if you **can**, answer **jú**, not *já*. *Talarðu ekki íslensku?* — *Jú, ég tala íslensku!* Icelandic has a special word for contradicting a negative, something English lacks (like French *si* or German *doch*).

grammars.title: Er að — the "-ing" form
body: The pattern is *vera* + *að* + the infinitive. Only the form of *vera* changes; the main verb stays put.
after: The difference from the plain form is small but real: *ég læri íslensku* means "I learn Icelandic" (in general, as an activity), while *ég er að læra íslensku* means "I'm learning Icelandic" (now, this very minute).
English uses *be* + *-ing* for exactly this, so you already think this way — the only new thing is the pattern.

blocks.text: Three words for one country, each with a different form. Language names are always written in **lowercase**; names of countries and nationalities always take a **capital**.

blocks.title: Two very Icelandic words
items: *Bandaríkin* literally means "the allied states" — note that Icelanders do **not** use the word "America" for the country. The habit of building their own words, mentioned in the foreword, works even on country names.
*Norðmaður* literally means "north-man"; *Þjóðverji* literally means "nation-defender". When a nationality doesn't look like its country's name, that's almost always why.

sections.title: Asking where people are from and where they live

blocks.text: Note that *hvar* (where) and *hvaðan* (where from) are two different words and can't be swapped. Icelandic also has *hvert* (where to), which appears in Unit 11 — three words where English mostly gets by with "where".

exercises.prompt: Make these sentences negative by putting *ekki* in the right place.
Fill in the right language or nationality.
items: Anna er frá Íslandi. Hún er ____.
Hann er frá Danmörku. Hann talar ____.
Ég er frá Indónesíu. Ég tala ____.
Þeir eru frá Þýskalandi. Þeir tala ____.
Hún er frá Frakklandi. Hún er ____.

exercises.prompt: Change to the "-ing" form with *er að*.

answers: Ég tala ekki þýsku. — Hún er ekki hér. — Við búum ekki í Jakarta. — Þú ert ekki kennari. — Ég skil þig ekki. — Þau eru ekki að læra.
Hvaðan ertu? — Ég bý í Reykjavík. — Ég tala ekki þýsku. — Ég er að læra íslensku. — Hvað ertu að gera? — Hvaða mál talar þú?
Ég er að læra íslensku. — Þú ert að lesa bók. — Hún er að tala í símann. — Við erum að borða. — Þeir eru að vinna.
